## Motivation {#motivation}

A detector can name the correct class while placing its box incorrectly, or find one object several times while missing another.
A detection result must identify both where an object is and which class it belongs to.
Its evaluation depends on matching predicted detections to reference objects under a stated protocol.

## Overlap and matching {#detection-metrics}

A detection metric is a numerical summary of predictions and reference annotations under an evaluation protocol.
It measures performance on that annotated dataset, rather than a property of a detector independent of the data and protocol.
Intersection over union compares a predicted [bounding box]{.term key="bounding-box"} $B$ with a reference $G$:

$$
  \operatorname{IoU}(B,G)=\frac{|B\cap G|}{|B\cup G|}.
$$

Here $|\cdot|$ denotes area, both boxes use the same coordinate system, and the union must have positive area.
IoU is a geometric overlap ratio; it contains no class-label or confidence information.

Precision and recall depend on which detections are matched to references.
Under a simple one-to-one, same-class matching protocol, a matched prediction is a true positive ($TP$), an unmatched prediction is a false positive ($FP$), and an unmatched reference is a false negative ($FN$).
The counts give

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{Precision}&=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\\
  \operatorname{Recall}&=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}.
  \end{aligned}
$$

These ratios require nonzero denominators; empty cases need the benchmark's stated convention.

## From ranked detections to average precision {#average-precision}

Detections are ranked by their [confidence scores]{.term key="confidence-score"}.
Admitting more predictions as the score threshold decreases produces different precision–recall points.
For one class, average precision summarises a precision–recall curve under a specified interpolation and matching protocol.
Mean AP averages over classes and, in some benchmarks, additional IoU thresholds.
VOC-style AP at IoU $0.5$ and COCO AP averaged over thresholds $0.50$ through $0.95$ are different metrics.
Do not compare numbers without their protocol; see the [COCO evaluation specification](https://cocodataset.org/#detection-eval).

## Example and evaluation boundaries {#applications}

Suppose an image contains three annotated objects of one class, and a detector returns three boxes.
With one-to-one matching at the chosen IoU threshold, suppose two boxes match different objects and the third duplicates the first object.
Then $TP=2$, $FP=1$, and $FN=1$, so precision and recall are both $2/3$.
The duplicate does not recover the missed object, even if its box overlaps an already matched object perfectly.
This example assumes ordinary objects without ignored or crowd annotations; the [COCO evaluator](https://github.com/cocodataset/cocoapi/blob/master/PythonAPI/pycocotools/cocoeval.py) includes additional matching and exclusion rules.

A single precision–recall point is not AP.
Report the matching threshold, class averaging, dataset split, and any size or maximum-detection restrictions alongside an AP value.
A detector with a higher AP need not have higher recall at every score threshold, so the deployed operating point still needs evaluation.

## Connections {#connections}

Two-stage detectors first propose regions and then classify and refine them, as in [Faster R-CNN](../../literature-review/vision/faster-r-cnn.qmd).
One-stage detectors produce detection predictions without that separate region-proposal stage, as in [YOLO](../../literature-review/vision/yolo.qmd) and [SSD](../../literature-review/vision/ssd.qmd).
[DETR](../../literature-review/vision/detr.qmd) adds a set-prediction and matching perspective.
